newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no need to change Hong Kong laws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no need to change Hong Kong laws.

text.p: The United States, backing Hong Kong governor Chris Patten, said on Friday it saw no need to toughen current laws in the territory as its future leader plans to do after China's takeover on July 1.
The future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, announced on Thursday a partial retreat from his plan to amend laws on political funding and public demonstrations after Britain hands back the territory to Beijing.
The new versions narrow a ban on foreign political funding and moderate limits on the right to protest. Nonetheless, opponents say the proposals are unchanged on essentials.
"The United States has believed very strongly that the existing ordinances adequately protect human and political rights in Hong Kong," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He said the revised proposals "do reflect some of the concerns expressed by the people of Hong Kong. But nevertheless, we don't see a reason to change the present laws."

"Politicians who were elected by the people drafted those laws," Burns told a news briefing. "And that's always better ... to have them drafted by democratically-elected politicians than by appointed officials."
Earlier, Patten told reporters in Hong Kong: "What still hasn't been addressed is the question of why these changes are necessary in the first place."
In addition to presiding over an easing of stiff colonial securities laws, Patten introduced electoral reforms that produced Hong Kong's first fully-elected legislature.

That legislature is to be replaced on July 1 with a provisional council appointed by a 400-member China-backed committee and the new body is expected to endorse the proposed tightening of civil liberties ordinances.
